items.definition: food that is prepared and eaten, usually at a particular time of day
exampleSentences: We always eat our evening meal together.
She skipped a meal because she was busy.
A good breakfast is an important meal.

items.definition: a small amount of food eaten between meals
exampleSentences: I usually have a snack in the afternoon.
She snacks on fruit when she's hungry.
We bought some snacks for the trip.

items.definition: food that remains after a meal and can be eaten later
exampleSentences: We had leftovers for lunch the next day.
I never throw away leftovers; I freeze them.
She turned the leftovers into a new dish.

items.definition: one of the foods that you use to make a particular dish
exampleSentences: Flour is the main ingredient in bread.
This recipe only needs five ingredients.
She checked that she had all the ingredients before cooking.

items.definition: a set of instructions for cooking a particular dish
exampleSentences: I found a new recipe for chicken soup.
This recipe takes about thirty minutes to make.
She shared her grandmother's recipe with me.

items.definition: the taste of a particular food or drink
exampleSentences: This soup has a wonderful flavor.
I love the flavor of fresh basil.
The sauce adds a lot of flavor to the dish.

items.definition: recently made, grown, or picked, and not frozen, dried, or preserved
exampleSentences: We buy fresh vegetables every week.
This bread is still fresh from the oven.
I prefer fresh fruit to canned fruit.

items.definition: having a very pleasant taste
exampleSentences: This cake is absolutely delicious.
The soup smelled delicious.
We had a delicious dinner at the new restaurant.

items.definition: having a strong, hot taste because of spices like pepper
exampleSentences: This curry is too spicy for me.
She loves spicy food.
The sauce was spicier than I expected.

items.definition: having the taste of sugar
exampleSentences: This cake is very sweet.
I don't usually like sweet drinks.
The fruit tasted sweeter than usual.

items.definition: a list of the food and drinks available in a restaurant
exampleSentences: Can I see the menu, please?
The menu has a lot of vegetarian options.
We looked at the menu before deciding what to order.

items.definition: a person whose job is to serve food and drinks in a restaurant
exampleSentences: The waiter brought us some water first.
We asked the waiter for the check.
A friendly waiter recommended the soup.

items.definition: an arrangement to have a table, room, or seat kept for you
exampleSentences: I made a reservation for eight o'clock.
Do we need a reservation for this restaurant?
She canceled her reservation at the last minute.

items.definition: a piece of paper that shows how much you must pay for a meal
exampleSentences: Could we have the check, please?
The waiter brought the check after dessert.
We split the check between the four of us.

items.definition: extra money you give to someone, like a waiter, for good service
exampleSentences: We left a generous tip for the waiter.
In some countries, people tip about fifteen percent.
She always tips well when the service is good.

items.definition: a small dish of food served before the main course
exampleSentences: We shared an appetizer before our main course.
The appetizer was small but tasty.
I always order an appetizer when I'm very hungry.

items.definition: the largest and most important dish of a meal
exampleSentences: I chose fish for my main course.
The main course included rice and vegetables.
For my main course, I'll have the pasta.

items.definition: sweet food eaten at the end of a meal
exampleSentences: We shared a chocolate dessert after dinner.
What's for dessert tonight?
She always saves room for dessert.

items.definition: to ask for food or drink in a restaurant
exampleSentences: I'd like to order the soup, please.
She ordered a salad and a coffee.
Have you decided what to order yet?

items.definition: a table set or reserved for two people in a restaurant
exampleSentences: We booked a table for two by the window.
Can we get a table for two, please?
The waiter showed us to a table for two near the door.
collocations: a table for two by the window

items.definition: a container, usually made of glass or plastic, used for keeping liquids
exampleSentences: I bought a bottle of water at the station.
She filled her bottle before the hike.
There are three empty bottles on the table.

items.definition: a container, usually made of glass, with a wide opening and a lid
exampleSentences: There's a jar of honey in the cupboard.
She keeps flour in a large jar.
Could you open this jar for me?

items.definition: a container made of cardboard or plastic, used for holding liquids or food
exampleSentences: We need a new carton of milk.
She threw the empty carton away.
There's an egg carton in the fridge.

items.definition: bread that has been shaped and baked in one whole piece
exampleSentences: I bought a fresh loaf of bread this morning.
She baked a loaf for the family dinner.
There's half a loaf left on the counter.

items.definition: a thin, flat piece cut from something larger, like bread or meat
exampleSentences: Could I have another slice of bread?
She cut the cake into eight slices.
He put a slice of cheese on his sandwich.

items.definition: the amount of food that is given to one person
exampleSentences: The portions at this restaurant are quite large.
She only eats small portions at dinner.
Could I have a smaller portion, please?

items.definition: a small amount of food that you put in your mouth at one time
exampleSentences: Can I have a bite of your sandwich?
She took a small bite of the cake.
He ate the apple in just a few bites.

items.definition: a small amount of a drink that you take into your mouth
exampleSentences: She took a sip of her coffee.
Can I have a sip of your juice?
He drank his tea in small sips.

items.definition: a very small amount of something, like salt, held between your fingers
exampleSentences: Add a pinch of salt to the soup.
She used just a pinch of sugar.
The recipe needs a pinch of pepper.

items.definition: a very small piece of bread, cake, or cookie
exampleSentences: There were crumbs all over the table.
He brushed the crumbs off his shirt.
A few crumbs fell from the sandwich.

lessons.title: Grammar: Countable and uncountable nouns: some, any, much, many

items.headword: Countable and uncountable nouns: some, any, much, many
items.definition: how to use some, any, much, many, a few, and a little with food nouns
items.explanationTR:
Countable nouns can be counted: one apple, two apples. Uncountable nouns cannot be counted with numbers, like rice, water, and bread; they don't usually have a plural form.

Some and any:
• Use 'some' in positive statements: There is some milk in the fridge. I bought some apples.
• Use 'any' in negatives and questions: There isn't any bread left. Do we have any eggs?

Much and many:
• Use 'many' with countable plural nouns: How many apples do you need? There aren't many eggs left.
• Use 'much' with uncountable nouns: How much milk is in the bottle? There isn't much sugar left.
• In everyday speech, 'a lot of' works with both: a lot of apples, a lot of milk.

A few and a little:
• 'A few' goes with countable nouns: I only have a few carrots.
• 'A little' goes with uncountable nouns: Add a little salt.

Remember: words like bread, rice, water, and information are usually uncountable in English, even when they seem countable in your own language.

questions.prompt: There is ---- juice in the fridge if you're thirsty.
questions.explanationTR: "Some" is used in positive statements; "juice" is uncountable, so "many" and "a few" are wrong, "any" belongs in negatives and questions, and "much" sounds unnatural in a simple positive statement.

questions.prompt: We don't have ---- eggs at all; the carton is empty.
questions.explanationTR: "Any" is used in negative sentences, and "at all" plus "the carton is empty" show there are zero eggs; "many" would suggest a few are left, and "much"/"a little" don't go with the countable noun "eggs."

questions.prompt: ---- apples do we need for the pie?
questions.explanationTR: "Apples" is a countable plural noun, so the question word is "how many"; "how much" is used only for uncountable nouns, and the other forms are not correct English questions.

questions.prompt: ---- sugar do you want in your coffee?
questions.explanationTR: "Sugar" is uncountable, so we ask "how much," not "how many," which is only for countable plural nouns.

questions.prompt: I only have ---- carrots, so I can't make a big salad.
questions.explanationTR: "Carrots" is countable, and "a few" means a small number, matching "can't make a big salad"; "many" would mean a large number, and "much"/"a little" are used only with uncountable nouns.

questions.prompt: There's only ---- rice left, so we should buy more soon.
questions.explanationTR: "Rice" is uncountable, and "a little" means a small amount, matching "we should buy more soon"; "a few" and "many" are used only with countable nouns, and "much" doesn't fit a positive statement like this.
In friendly offers, we use "some" even in questions ("Would you like some coffee?"); "any" is used in ordinary questions, not offers.

questions.prompt: Could you buy ---- on your way home? We need it for sandwiches.
questions.explanationTR: "Bread" is uncountable, so we say "some bread" (or "a loaf of bread"), not "a bread" or "two breads"; "many" and "a few" go only with countable plural nouns.

items.definition: Short restaurant dialogues and eight questions about what to say next

questions.prompt:
A: Are you ready to order?
B: ----
A: Great choice! I'll bring that right out.
options: No, the bill was too expensive.
Yes, I left a big tip last time.
Yes, I'll have the grilled chicken, please.
No, I don't have a reservation.
questions.explanationTR: This is the only option that actually places an order, which matches A's reply, "Great choice! I'll bring that right out."

questions.prompt:
A: How many people is the reservation for?
B: ----
A: Perfect, I have a table for two ready.
options: The soup was too spicy for me.
Can we get some more water?
Just two of us, thank you.
questions.explanationTR: The question asks for a number of people, and this option gives that number, matching A's "table for two."

questions.prompt:
A: Would you like to see the dessert menu?
B: ----
A: I recommend the chocolate cake — it's our best dessert.
options: No, we don't have a reservation.
Yes, please. What do you recommend?
No, the check is too high.
Yes, I'd like a table for two.
questions.explanationTR: B asks for a recommendation, and A answers by recommending the chocolate cake; the other options don't answer an offer of the dessert menu.

questions.prompt:
A: Is everything okay with your meal?
B: ----
A: I'm glad you're enjoying it!
options: Yes, can we have the check, please?
No, the waiter hasn't come yet.
Yes, everything is delicious, thank you.
Yes, I'd like to order a dessert.
questions.explanationTR: This option directly says the food is good, matching A's response, "I'm glad you're enjoying it"; the other yes-answers change the subject instead of describing the meal.

questions.prompt:
A: Excuse me, could we have the check, please?
B: ----
A: Thank you so much.
options: Of course, I'll bring it right away.
No, we're out of that dish.
Sure, would you like a reservation?
questions.explanationTR: This option directly agrees to bring the check, which fits A's grateful reply, "Thank you so much"; the other options answer a different request, like the menu or a table.

questions.prompt:
A: This soup is amazing! What's in it?
B: ----
A: That explains the wonderful flavor.
options: It comes with a side salad.
We're out of that dish today.
It has fresh basil and a few other spices.
questions.explanationTR: The question asks what is in the soup, and only this option names ingredients, which matches A's comment about the "wonderful flavor."

questions.prompt:
A: Should we leave a tip?
B: ----
A: Sounds fair — the service was great.
options: No, we already paid the reservation.
No, the appetizer was too small.
Yes, let's leave about fifteen percent.
questions.explanationTR: This option agrees to leave a tip and gives an amount, matching A's comment about the tip being "fair" because of good service.

questions.prompt:
A: Do you have a table for two available?
B: ----
A: Thank you, we'll wait.
options: Not right now, but there will be one in ten minutes.
Yes, would you like the dessert menu?
questions.explanationTR: This option gives a wait time, which matches A's reply, "we'll wait"; the other options don't explain why the customers would need to wait.
